newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: U.S. to open anti-drug office in Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to open anti-drug office in Nicaragua.

text.p: The United States has agreed to open an anti-drug office this year in Nicaragua, a growing transit point for South American drugs heading to the United States, a U.S. State Department report said on Monday.

"At the request of the Nicaraguan government, the government of the United States has agreed to open a DEA (Drug Enforcement Administration) office in Managua in 1997," said the report, released by the U.S. Embassy in Managua.
Nicaragua, which was ruled by the pro-Cuban Sandinista government from 1979 to 1990, was the only country in Latin America besides Cuba without a DEA office.

But the election of a pro-U.S. government in 1990 slowly brought renewed cooperation between U.S. and Nicaraguan anti-drug forces. Earlier this year, former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega failed in his bid for a political comeback when he lost the presidential race to right-winger Arnoldo Aleman.
The decision to open a DEA office here came after a successful three-month test last year in cooperation between the two countries' anti-drug forces, the report said.

It attributed the rise in drug trafficking in Nicaragua, the second poorest country in Latin America, to a lack of financing for anti-drug forces, a faulty judicial system and a lack of police training.
It said the main transit point for drugs passing through Nicaragua was its sparsely populated, under-policed Atlantic coast, which it described as "a haven for Colombian drug traffickers."
Drug traffickers move the drugs to Nicaragua's Atlantic coast in speed boats, then ship it north over land in cargo containers of perishable food, it added.

The report lauded the November 1996 seizure of 400 kilos of cocaine near Corn Island off Nicaragua's Atlantic coast in a joint U.S.-Nicaraguan operation, but criticised an easy-to-intimidate judicial system that often allows drug traffickers to walk free.
